analysis.one_liner: Boosts Social Security checks with a seniors' inflation index and removes the cap on wages taxed for Social Security.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised Social Security cost-of-living adjustments and phased out the $132,900 cap on wages taxed for Social Security, died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how Social Security cost-of-living adjustments are calculated, using a new inflation index built around what people 62 and older actually buy — mainly health care — instead of the index for urban wage earners. It would also gradually phase out, and after 2025 eliminate, the cap on wages subject to Social Security payroll taxes ($132,900 in 2019), so high earners and the self-employed would pay the tax on all their earnings. The newly taxed earnings would earn only a small extra benefit credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries, who would get larger and more accurate annual cost-of-living increases, since the elderly-specific index typically rises faster than the index now used. The program's finances would also be strengthened because all wages, not just the first ~$133,000, would be taxed. Lower- and middle-wage workers would see no new taxes, since the change only applies to earnings above the cap.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and program solvency

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers and requires Social Security to use it for cost-of-living adjustments, replacing the index for urban wage earners that understates costs seniors face, particularly for health care.

Phases out the cap on wages and self-employment income subject to Social Security taxes — 86% of earnings above the cap taxed in 2020, shrinking each year to 0% after 2025 — so high earners would pay Social Security tax on their full income.
Adds the newly taxed earnings into the benefit formula at very low rates (3% and 0.25% factors), giving high earners a modest benefit increase in return for their much larger contributions.

Specifies that any benefit increase from the new index cannot count as income or resources when determining eligibility for Supplemental Security Income or Medicaid, so the higher checks would not cost poor beneficiaries other aid.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and self-employed people earning above the Social Security wage cap, who would pay the 12.4% combined Social Security tax on their entire income after the phase-out, while receiving only a small additional benefit in return. In 2019 that cap was $132,900.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the wage cap

drawbacks.text: High earners and self-employed professionals would see a large tax increase: the Social Security tax would apply to their full income rather than stopping at the cap, with the extra benefit credit (3% and 0.25% factors) returning only a small fraction of what they pay in.

The elderly-specific inflation index would raise benefits for all beneficiaries, adding to program costs — a cost an honest supporter would weigh against the new revenue, and one critics say outpaces measured inflation for some households.

Fully removing the cap breaks the long-standing link between what top earners pay into Social Security and what they get out, which opponents argue changes Social Security from earned insurance toward a redistribution program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: larger, more accurate cost-of-living increases for tens of millions of beneficiaries and a stronger funding base for the program. The costs fall on a narrow group — earners above roughly $133,000 — which is exactly why the bill had a hard path: the people paying the bill are also among the most politically engaged. The main design criticism is that the bill gives high earners very little back in benefits, making the tax change close to a pure transfer; supporters would call that the point.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees, none of which ever held a hearing or markup on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Deutch introduced the bill on April 12, 2019, with seven original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The same day, the House referred it to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and Labor Committees, and it was sent to the Ways and Means Social Security Subcommittee.
On April 15, 2019, part of it was also referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No committee or subcommittee took any further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the Social Security wage cap, who never had to pay tax on their full earnings, and the Ways and Means Committee leadership, which never had to take a recorded position on a payroll tax increase.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the wage cap

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee of primary referral never held a markup or hearing; the bill sat in the Social Security Subcommittee for the entire Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held; the sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on, so the bill's fate was decided by inaction rather than by a recorded party split.

industries.industry: Highest-earning households (wages and self-employment income above the cap)
industries.note: They would pay the 12.4% combined Social Security tax on their entire income after the phase-out, while the bill credits the extra contributions back at only 3% and 0.25% rates. Their interest in this bill runs directly against beneficiaries' larger checks.
